Chapter Seven: The Long Game—Sustaining Change Over Months and Years
You know that first wave of excitement when you start a new habit? That spark of hope that says, "This time, it's going to stick."
Everything feels possible at the beginning. But as the days turn into weeks, and those weeks stretch into months, the shine starts to wear off. Real life doesn’t exactly stop so you can work on yourself—there are work deadlines, family obligations, and those little surprises that always seem to pop up.
Picture this: a small business owner, fired up to keep his daily exercise routine. But as the holidays get closer, his schedule fills up, and suddenly, the gym feels miles away. The couch? It’s calling his name.
Then he remembers something a friend once said: “Don’t break the chain.” Instead of chasing perfection, he shifts his focus to just showing up. On crazy days, he might only do a few quick stretches or take a brisk walk around the block. Sure, it’s not always impressive, but it keeps his momentum going.
Here’s the thing—a lot of us underestimate the power of simply showing up, even when things aren’t perfect. It’s easy to think that missing a day means you’ve failed and have to start all over. But that’s not how progress works. It’s not about being flawless; it’s about sticking with it, especially when life gets messy.
Let’s take another example—a teacher who’s passionate about learning new languages. She sets a small goal for herself: just ten minutes of practice each day. Some days, she does more. Other days, it’s a mad dash to squeeze it in before bed. But as the months roll by, she’s amazed at how much she’s actually learned. That steady, gentle effort builds up, and before she knows it, she feels genuinely accomplished.
So, what’s the secret to playing the long game? It’s not about going all out every single day. It’s about consistent, gentle effort—day after day. When you allow yourself some flexibility and focus on simply not breaking the chain, your habits start to become a natural part of your life. They stick around, even when things get unpredictable.
Here’s the key takeaway: The long game isn’t about intensity. It’s about weaving small, steady actions into your routine so they can survive the ups and downs of real life.
